techniques.name: Federated Learning
techniques.description: Federated learning enables collaborative model training across multiple distributed parties (devices, organisations, or data centres) without requiring centralised data sharing. Participants train models locally on their private datasets and only share model updates (gradients, weights, or aggregated statistics) with a central coordinator. This distributed approach serves multiple purposes: preserving data privacy and sovereignty, reducing communication costs, enabling learning from diverse data sources, improving model robustness through heterogeneous training, and facilitating compliance with data protection regulations whilst maintaining model performance comparable to centralised training.

example_use_cases.description: Developing a smartphone keyboard prediction model by learning from users' typing patterns without their text ever leaving their devices, enabling personalised predictions whilst maintaining complete data privacy.

Training a medical diagnosis model across multiple hospitals without sharing patient records, ensuring model robustness by learning from diverse patient populations and clinical practices across different institutions.

limitations.description: Communication overhead can be substantial, especially with frequent model updates and large models, potentially limiting scalability and increasing training time compared to centralised approaches.

Statistical heterogeneity across participants (non-IID data distributions) can lead to training instability, slower convergence, and reduced model performance compared to centralised training on pooled data.
System heterogeneity in computational capabilities, network connectivity, and availability of participating devices can create bottlenecks and introduce bias towards more capable participants.
Privacy vulnerabilities remain through gradient leakage attacks, model inversion, and membership inference attacks that can potentially reconstruct sensitive information from shared model updates.
Coordination complexity increases with the number of participants, requiring sophisticated aggregation protocols, fault tolerance mechanisms, and secure communication infrastructure.

resources.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data
resources.abstract: Modern mobile devices have access to a wealth of data suitable for learning models, which in turn can greatly improve the user experience on the device. For example, language models can improve speech recognition and text entry, and image models can automatically select good photos. However, this rich data is often privacy sensitive, large in quantity, or both, which may preclude logging to the data center and training there using conventional approaches. We advocate an alternative that leaves the training data distributed on the mobile devices, and learns a shared model by aggregating locally-computed updates. We term this decentralized approach Federated Learning. We present a practical method for the federated learning of deep networks based on iterative model averaging, and conduct an extensive empirical evaluation, considering five different model architectures and four datasets. These experiments demonstrate the approach is robust to the unbalanced and non-IID data distributions that are a defining characteristic of this setting. Communication costs are the principal constraint, and we show a reduction in required communication rounds by 10-100x as compared to synchronized stochastic gradient descent.

resources.title: Federated Learning - DeepLearning.AI
Federated learning for predicting clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19
resources.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a method used for training artificial intelligence models with data from multiple sources while maintaining data anonymity, thus removing many barriers to data sharing. Here we used data from 20 institutes across the globe to train a FL model, called EXAM (electronic medical record (EMR) chest X-ray AI model), that predicts the future oxygen requirements of symptomatic patients with COVID-19 using inputs of vital signs, laboratory data and chest X-rays. EXAM achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) >0.92 for predicting outcomes at 24 and 72 h from the time of initial presentation to the emergency room, and it provided 16% improvement in average AUC measured across all participating sites and an average increase in generalizability of 38% when compared with models trained at a single site using that site's data. For prediction of mechanical ventilation treatment or death at 24 h at the largest independent test site, EXAM achieved a sensitivity of 0.950 and specificity of 0.882. In this study, FL facilitated rapid data science collaboration without data exchange and generated a model that generalized across heterogeneous, unharmonized datasets for prediction of clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19, setting the stage for the broader use of FL in healthcare.

resources.title: Federated learning enables big data for rare cancer boundary detection
resources.abstract: Although machine learning (ML) has shown promise across disciplines, out-of-sample generalizability is concerning. This is currently addressed by sharing multi-site data, but such centralization is challenging/infeasible to scale due to various limitations. Federated ML (FL) provides an alternative paradigm for accurate and generalizable ML, by only sharing numerical model updates. Here we present the largest FL study to-date, involving data from 71 sites across 6 continents, to generate an automatic tumor boundary detector for the rare disease of glioblastoma, reporting the largest such dataset in the literature ( n = 6, 314). We demonstrate a 33% delineation improvement for the surgically targetable tumor, and 23% for the complete tumor extent, over a publicly trained model. We anticipate our study to: 1) enable more healthcare studies informed by large diverse data, ensuring meaningful results for rare diseases and underrepresented populations, 2) facilitate further analyses for glioblastoma by releasing our consensus model, and 3) demonstrate the FL effectiveness at such scale and task-complexity as a paradigm shift for multi-site collaborations, alleviating the need for data-sharing.

sample_claims.text: The model training process does not require patient data to leave individual healthcare institutions
The diagnostic model performs reliably despite learning from patient populations with heterogeneous clinical characteristics across multiple sites
The keyboard prediction model learns from user typing patterns without transmitting personal text content to central servers

techniques.name: Runtime Monitoring and Circuit Breakers
techniques.description: Runtime monitoring and circuit breakers observe a deployed AI service and restrict model calls when configured signals breach specified limits. In the closed state, requests pass through and recent failures are counted, while an open breaker rejects requests or provides a configured fallback, such as a cached answer, a simpler model, a rule-based default or referral to a person. After a waiting period, the half-open state permits a few trial calls and closes again only if they succeed. Model-related triggers can include immediately available signals such as input-drift scores (how far incoming data has moved from the training data) or low prediction confidence, since accuracy usually needs later outcome labels. Logs record state changes and triggering signals, supporting review of why the service was restricted without guaranteeing that the fallback is safe.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's diagnostic-support service stops showing model suggestions to clinicians when the share of low-confidence predictions or the input drift score passes preset limits, for example after a scanner software update changes the images. A notice tells staff the standard workflow applies until engineers reset the breaker.

Deploying runtime monitoring for a recommendation engine that tracks recommendation diversity, click-through rates, and user engagement patterns, automatically switching to simpler algorithms when complex models show signs of performance degradation or unusual behaviour patterns.

A bank's credit-scoring service records every breaker state change, the metric that triggered it and the fallback used in an audit log. Model risk reviewers read the log each month to see how often, when and why the model was restricted, and whether the thresholds need revisiting.

An airline's customer-service assistant is wrapped in a circuit breaker that counts timeouts, blocked outputs and refusals. When they pass a limit after a faulty release, traffic switches to a scripted menu and the on-call engineer is paged, so the faulty version is stopped quickly without waiting for a manual decision.

limitations.description: Thresholds are hard to set. Too tight and the breaker trips on normal variation and withdraws a working service. Too loose and it stays closed through a real failure. Good settings need historical data from the live system, which is scarce at launch.

Model-level triggers are proxies for correctness. Drift scores and confidence can look normal while the model is confidently wrong, so a breaker that never trips is not evidence that predictions are right.

Gradual degradation and slow attacks can stay inside the limits, because each reading is acceptable while the cumulative effect is harmful. Catching them needs separate trend analysis or delayed accuracy checks alongside the breaker.

The breaker only moves the risk to the fallback. A cached answer, a simpler model or a human referral must itself be tested, and referral fails if reviewers cannot absorb a sudden diversion of traffic.

Tripping has a cost. A false trip withdraws a working service from users who may depend on it in time-critical settings, and reopening after a fixed cooldown, or on a few easy trial requests, can restore traffic before the underlying fault is fixed.

resources.title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems
resources.abstract: Machine learning offers a fantastically powerful toolkit for building useful complexprediction systems quickly. This paper argues it is dangerous to think ofthese quick wins as coming for free. Using the software engineering frameworkof technical debt, we find it is common to incur massive ongoing maintenancecosts in real-world ML systems. We explore several ML-specific risk factors toaccount for in system design. These include boundary erosion, entanglement,hidden feedback loops, undeclared consumers, data dependencies, configurationissues, changes in the external world, and a variety of system-level anti-patterns.

resources.title: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor: A System for Real-Time Insights into Deployed Machine Learning Models
resources.abstract: With the increasing adoption of machine learning (ML) models and systems in high-stakes settings across different industries, guaranteeing a model's performance after deployment has become crucial. Monitoring models in production is a critical aspect of ensuring their continued performance and reliability. We present Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor, a fully managed service that continuously monitors the quality of machine learning models hosted on Amazon SageMaker. Our system automatically detects data, concept, bias, and feature attribution drift in models in real-time and provides alerts so that model owners can take corrective actions and thereby maintain high quality models. We describe the key requirements obtained from customers, system design and architecture, and methodology for detecting different types of drift. Further, we provide quantitative evaluations followed by use cases, insights, and lessons learned from more than two years of production deployment.

sample_claims.text: The diagnostic-support service stops showing model suggestions to clinicians when the share of low-confidence predictions or the input drift score passes its preset limit, and the standard clinical workflow applies until the breaker is reset.
The fraud-scoring service keeps answering requests during a model fault because the breaker diverts traffic to a rules-based fallback once the failure rate passes its threshold.
The forecasting service falls back to a simple baseline forecast when its inputs leave their historical ranges, so downstream users do not receive out-of-range forecasts.
Every breaker state change is recorded with its time, the metric that triggered it and the fallback used, and the log is available to system owners and auditors.
The platform records when its configured runtime restrictions activate and when normal calls resume.

techniques.name: MLflow Experiment Tracking
techniques.description: MLflow is an open-source platform that tracks machine learning experiments by automatically logging parameters, metrics, models, and artifacts throughout the ML lifecycle. It provides a centralised repository for comparing different experimental runs, reproducing results, and managing model versions. Teams can track hyperparameters, evaluation metrics, model files, and execution environment details, creating a comprehensive audit trail that supports collaboration, reproducibility, and regulatory compliance across the entire machine learning development process.

example_use_cases.description: Tracking medical diagnosis model experiments across different hospitals, logging hyperparameters, performance metrics, and model artifacts to ensure reproducible research and enable regulatory audits of model development processes.

Managing fraud detection model versions in production, tracking which specific model configuration and training data version is deployed, enabling quick rollback and performance comparison when system reliability issues arise.

Documenting loan approval model experiments with complete parameter tracking and performance logging across demographic groups, supporting fair lending compliance by providing transparent records of model development and validation processes.

limitations.description: Requires teams to adopt disciplined logging practices and may introduce overhead to development workflows if not properly integrated into existing processes.
Storage costs can grow substantially with extensive artifact logging, especially for large models or high-frequency experimentation.
Tracking quality depends on developers consistently logging relevant information, with incomplete logging leading to gaps in experimental records.
Complex multi-stage pipelines may require custom instrumentation to capture dependencies and data flow relationships effectively.
Security and access control configurations require careful setup to protect sensitive model information and experimental data in shared environments.

resources.title: Accelerating the Machine Learning Lifecycle with MLflow
resources.abstract: Machine learning development creates multiple new challenges that are not present in a traditional software development lifecycle. These include keeping track of the myriad inputs to an ML application (e.g., data versions, code and tuning parameters), reproducing results, and production deployment. In this paper, we summarize these challenges from our experience with Databricks customers, and describe MLflow, an open source platform we recently launched to streamline the machine learning lifecycle. MLflow covers three key challenges: experimentation, reproducibility, and model deployment, using generic APIs that work with any ML library, algorithm and programming language. The project has a rapidly growing open source community, with over 50 contributors since its launch in June 2018.

resources.title: MLflow Tracking Quickstart
An MLOps Framework for Explainable Network Intrusion Detection with MLflow
resources.abstract: The surge in network traffic has required advanced techniques to ensure network security. Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs), which increasingly employ Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) methodologies, play a pivotal role in this task by continuously monitoring network traffic patterns and identifying suspicious activities. To address the complexities of developing ML- and DL-based NIDS, MLOps tools have been designed to optimize model deployment, monitoring, and management in production environments, streamlining model development. These tools enable efficient experimentation, version management, and logging of artifacts for network administrators and data scientists. In this work, we design a framework powered by MLflow to manage the ML pipeline from data handling to results visualization. To show the effectiveness of our framework, we conducted an experimental campaign on 4 broadly used security datasets (viz. NSL-KDD, IoT-23, Kitsune, and TON_IoT) performing crucial tasks for intrusion detection, namely anomaly detection, binary misuse detection, and multiclass misuse detection.

resources.title: Enhancing Quantum Software Development Process with Experiment Tracking
resources.abstract: As quantum computing advances from theoretical promise to experimental reality, the need for rigorous experiment tracking becomes critical. Drawing inspiration from best practices in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI), we argue that reproducibility, scalability, and collaboration in quantum research can benefit significantly from structured tracking workflows. This paper explores the application of MLflow in quantum research, illustrating how it enables better development practices, experiment reproducibility, decision making, and cross-domain integration in an increasingly hybrid classical-quantum landscape.

sample_claims.text: All experimental configurations and hyperparameters tested during model development are centrally logged with their corresponding performance outcomes
The deployed clinical model is reproducible from logged training parameters, data versions, and execution environment specifications
The fraud detection model's performance evolution across successive training runs is traceable through logged metrics and artifact histories
The production model version can be systematically compared against alternative experimental configurations evaluated during development
Model training artifacts and evaluation metrics are accessible to authorized team members through a centralized repository supporting collaborative review

techniques.name: Data Version Control
techniques.description: Data Version Control (DVC) is a Git-like version control system specifically designed for machine learning data, models, and experiments. It tracks changes to large data files, maintains reproducible ML pipelines, and creates a complete audit trail of data transformations, model training, and evaluation processes. DVC works alongside Git to provide end-to-end lineage tracking from raw data through preprocessing, training, and deployment, enabling teams to reproduce any model version and understand exactly how datasets evolved throughout the ML lifecycle.

example_use_cases.description: Tracking medical imaging dataset versions and model training pipelines to ensure reproducible research results, enabling hospitals to verify which specific data version and preprocessing steps were used for regulatory submissions.

Managing credit scoring model data pipelines with complete version control of training datasets, feature engineering steps, and model artifacts, ensuring reliable model reproduction and rollback capabilities when performance issues arise.

Maintaining pharmaceutical drug discovery data lineage across multiple research teams, tracking compound datasets, feature extraction processes, and model versions to support FDA submissions with complete experimental provenance.

limitations.description: Requires learning Git-like workflows and CLI commands, which may have a steep learning curve for teams unfamiliar with version control systems.
Storage costs can be substantial for large datasets with frequent changes, especially when maintaining multiple versions and branches of data.
Complex data pipelines with many interdependencies may require significant setup time and careful configuration to track properly.
Performance can degrade with very large files or datasets due to checksumming and synchronisation overhead during operations.
Team coordination becomes essential as improper branch management or merge conflicts can disrupt collaborative workflows.

resources.title: Get Started with DVC
On the Co-evolution of ML Pipelines and Source Code - Empirical Study of DVC Projects
resources.abstract: The growing popularity of machine learning (ML) applications has led to the introduction of software engineering tools such as Data Versioning Control (DVC), MLFlow and Pachyderm that enable versioning ML data, models, pipelines and model evaluation metrics. Since these versioned ML artifacts need to be synchronized not only with each other, but also with the source and test code of the software applications into which the models are integrated, prior findings on co-evolution and coupling between software artifacts might need to be revisited. Hence, in order to understand the degree of coupling between ML-related and other software artifacts, as well as the adoption of ML versioning features, this paper empirically studies the usage of DVC in 391 Github projects, 25 of which in detail. Our results show that more than half of the DVC files in a project are changed at least once every one-tenth of the project's lifetime. Furthermore, we observe a tight coupling between DVC files and other artifacts, with 1/4 pull requests changing source code and 1/2 pull requests changing tests requiring a change to DVC files. As additional evidence of the observed complexity associated with adopting ML-related software engineering tools like DVC, an average of 78% of the studied projects showed a non-constant trend in pipeline complexity.

resources.title: DVC in Open Source ML-development: The Action and the Reaction
resources.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) systems are gaining popularity, reshaping various domains ranging from customer services to software engineering. The effectiveness of ML systems is dependent on the quality of their training data. Therefore, practitioners invest substantial time experimenting with different data, parameters, and models to guarantee the quality of the end system. Prior work highlighted unique challenges of developing ML systems, particularly concerning versioning data and models. Recently, various tools such as DVC and MLFlow have emerged to aid developers in the storage and tracking of data. Despite their growing popularity, very little is known about their usage patterns and impact on open-source software (OSS) systems. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study on 56 GitHub OSS projects that use DVC to understand the DVC usage pattern and the impact of using DVC on the software development process. We found that Versioning and tracking is the most adopted DVC feature, being utilized by all 56 projects and being the only adopted feature in 85.7% of them. Furthermore, we found that DVC has a significant impact on the software development process indicators such as the number of created pull requests (PRs), and the number of bug-fix commits. For instance, our findings showed that DVC causes a peak in the number of commits and PRs at the moment of the adoption, followed by a long-term decrease. We believe that our findings can assist practitioners in tailoring tools to better meet user requirements and help organizations realize potential outcomes of adopting such tools.

sample_claims.text: The training dataset's lineage is traceable from original data sources through all preprocessing transformations to the deployed model
The model's performance can be recreated using the exact dataset version and pipeline configuration from any prior release
All modifications to sensor calibration data and feature extraction steps are documented with timestamps and author attribution
The system can be rolled back to any previous data processing pipeline version when performance degradation is detected
The complete history of dataset changes is preserved and queryable across the model's development lifecycle

techniques.name: API Usage Pattern Monitoring
techniques.description: API usage pattern monitoring examines how each account uses a deployed model's API, to catch misuse that no single request reveals. The monitor keeps a running record per account and compares it with a baseline of normal use, raising an alert when the account departs from it. Published detectors for model theft show two ways to do this: one tests whether the distances between an account's successive queries follow the bell-shaped pattern that ordinary use produces, and another estimates how much of the model's behaviour the account's queries and responses would let someone rebuild. Providers also score how often an account triggers content filters or repeats jailbreak attempts, and send high scores for review. The output is a log of alerts and the actions taken, which gives a dated record of how the API was used compared with the uses it was approved for.

example_use_cases.description: A fraud-scoring API provider examines each client's query stream for runs of near-identical transactions altered in small steps, which suggest someone is probing for the score at which a transaction passes. Flagged accounts are rate-limited and sent to the security team for review.

A company selling traffic-sign recognition as a paid API tests whether the spacing between each customer's successive image queries follows the pattern ordinary use produces. Accounts whose queries look synthetic and widely spread, as in model-copying attacks, are flagged for investigation and possible suspension.

A health-technology company serving a paediatric triage model to many clinics monitors each clinic's query volumes and the ages in its requests. A clinic sending mostly adult patients, or a sudden change after a software update, is flagged so the company can contact it before unsafe advice is given.

A provider of a text-generation API scores each customer's usage by how often prompts and responses are flagged as harmful and whether jailbreak attempts recur. Customers with high scores go to review, which can lead to a warning or suspension.

A bank's model risk team compares the monthly log of calls to its credit-scoring API, by internal team and purpose, with the uses approved at validation. The comparison is filed in the model's audit record, so reviewers can see whether the model is used as documented.

limitations.description: Anomalies are defined against a baseline of normal use, and ordinary users can be unusual. In PRADA's tests, legitimate queries made of consecutive frames from a sequence triggered false alarms at stricter settings, so the alert threshold has to be tuned to each model and use case.

A patient attacker can stay inside normal limits by querying slowly, adding dummy queries or spreading queries across many accounts. PRADA's authors show that padding queries raises the attacker's cost three to ten times, and that multiple accounts defeat per-account analysis.

Useful monitoring needs request content, or features of it, to be logged and sometimes read by reviewers. For sensitive applications that may be unlawful or unacceptable, and Microsoft notes that detection may be less accurate when human review is switched off for such customers.

Detectors keep state for every account. PRADA's authors estimate a few gigabytes in total for a few hundred clients of an image model, and the cost rises with traffic and with the retention period set for audit evidence.

The published extraction detectors were tested on small models, decision trees in one case and image classifiers in the other, against simulated attackers. Kesarwani et al. describe their warning as approximate, so an alert is a lead for investigation, not proof of theft.

resources.title: Model Extraction Warning in MLaaS Paradigm
resources.abstract: Machine learning models deployed on the cloud are susceptible to several security threats including extraction attacks. Adversaries may abuse a model's prediction API to steal the model thus compromising model confidentiality, privacy of training data, and revenue from future query payments. This work introduces a model extraction monitor that quantifies the extraction status of models by continually observing the API query and response streams of users. We present two novel strategies that measure either the information gain or the coverage of the feature space spanned by user queries to estimate the learning rate of individual and colluding adversaries. Both approaches have low computational overhead and can easily be offered as services to model owners to warn them against state of the art extraction attacks. We demonstrate empirical performance results of these approaches for decision tree and neural network models using open source datasets and BigML MLaaS platform.

resources.title: PRADA: Protecting Against DNN Model Stealing Attacks
resources.abstract: Machine learning (ML) applications are increasingly prevalent. Protecting the confidentiality of ML models becomes paramount for two reasons: (a) a model can be a business advantage to its owner, and (b) an adversary may use a stolen model to find transferable adversarial examples that can evade classification by the original model. Access to the model can be restricted to be only via well-defined prediction APIs. Nevertheless, prediction APIs still provide enough information to allow an adversary to mount model extraction attacks by sending repeated queries via the prediction API. In this paper, we describe new model extraction attacks using novel approaches for generating synthetic queries, and optimizing training hyperparameters. Our attacks outperform state-of-the-art model extraction in terms of transferability of both targeted and non-targeted adversarial examples (up to +29-44 percentage points, pp), and prediction accuracy (up to +46 pp) on two datasets. We provide take-aways on how to perform effective model extraction attacks. We then propose PRADA, the first step towards generic and effective detection of DNN model extraction attacks. It analyzes the distribution of consecutive API queries and raises an alarm when this distribution deviates from benign behavior. We show that PRADA can detect all prior model extraction attacks with no false positives.

sample_claims.text: The fraud API logs alerts from the configured query-distance detector so the security team can investigate suspected extraction-style sequences.
The clinical assistant records recurring harmful-content classifier flags by frequency and severity for the stated monitoring period.
The education API makes its request-volume summaries, monitoring settings and alert histories available for review of actual usage.
The moderation API records recurring harmful-content signals and the resulting safety-review alerts.

techniques.name: Model Extraction Defence Testing
techniques.description: Model extraction defence testing evaluates protections against attackers who attempt to steal model functionality by querying it and training surrogate models. This technique assesses defences like query limiting, output perturbation, watermarking, and fingerprinting by simulating extraction attacks and measuring how much model functionality can be replicated. Testing evaluates both the effectiveness of defences in preventing extraction and their impact on legitimate use cases, ensuring security measures don't excessively degrade user experience.

example_use_cases.description: Testing protections for a proprietary fraud detection API to ensure competitors cannot recreate the model's decision boundaries through systematic querying, by simulating extraction attacks using query budgets, active learning strategies, and substitute model training.

Evaluating whether rate limiting and output obfuscation for an automated essay grading API prevent competitors from extracting the scoring model through systematic submission of probe essays designed to reverse-engineer grading criteria.

Testing whether a traffic prediction API's defensive perturbations prevent extraction of the underlying routing optimization model whilst maintaining sufficient accuracy for legitimate urban planning applications.

limitations.description: Sophisticated attackers may use transfer learning, active learning, or knowledge distillation to extract models with 10-50x fewer queries than static defences anticipate, and can adapt their strategies as they probe defences, requiring dynamic rather than static protection mechanisms.
Defensive measures like output perturbation can degrade model utility for legitimate users, creating tension between security and usability.
Difficult to distinguish between legitimate high-volume use and malicious extraction attempts, potentially blocking valid users.
Watermarking and fingerprinting techniques may be removed or obscured by attackers who post-process extracted models.

Difficult to validate defence effectiveness without exposing the model to actual extraction attempts, and limited public benchmarks make it challenging to compare defence strategies objectively across different model types and threat scenarios.

Requires specialised expertise in adversarial machine learning and attack simulation to design realistic extraction scenarios, making it challenging for organisations without dedicated security teams to implement comprehensive testing.

resources.title: Stealing Machine Learning Models via Prediction APIs
resources.abstract: Machine learning (ML) models may be deemed confidential due to their sensitive training data, commercial value, or use in security applications. Increasingly often, confidential ML models are being deployed with publicly accessible query interfaces. ML-as-a-service ("predictive analytics") systems are an example: Some allow users to train models on potentially sensitive data and charge others for access on a pay-per-query basis. The tension between model confidentiality and public access motivates our investigation of model extraction attacks. In such attacks, an adversary with black-box access, but no prior knowledge of an ML model's parameters or training data, aims to duplicate the functionality of (i.e., "steal") the model. Unlike in classical learning theory settings, ML-as-a-service offerings may accept partial feature vectors as inputs and include confidence values with predictions. Given these practices, we show simple, efficient attacks that extract target ML models with near-perfect fidelity for popular model classes including logistic regression, neural networks, and decision trees. We demonstrate these attacks against the online services of BigML and Amazon Machine Learning. We further show that the natural countermeasure of omitting confidence values from model outputs still admits potentially harmful model extraction attacks. Our results highlight the need for careful ML model deployment and new model extraction countermeasures.

resources.title: Stealing Part of a Production Language Model
resources.abstract: We introduce the first model-stealing attack that extracts precise, nontrivial information from black-box production language models like OpenAI's ChatGPT or Google's PaLM-2. Specifically, our attack recovers the embedding projection layer (up to symmetries) of a transformer model, given typical API access. For under \$20 USD, our attack extracts the entire projection matrix of OpenAI's Ada and Babbage language models. We thereby confirm, for the first time, that these black-box models have a hidden dimension of 1024 and 2048, respectively. We also recover the exact hidden dimension size of the gpt-3.5-turbo model, and estimate it would cost under $2,000 in queries to recover the entire projection matrix. We conclude with potential defenses and mitigations, and discuss the implications of possible future work that could extend our attack.

sample_claims.text: The proprietary fraud detection API withstands systematic querying attempts designed to replicate its decision boundaries without degrading service for legitimate users
The model service distinguishes between legitimate high-volume use and malicious extraction attempts through behavioral analysis
The autonomous vehicle perception API maintains protection against competitors extracting routing optimization logic through probe queries across varied traffic scenarios

techniques.name: Multi-Agent System Testing
techniques.description: Multi-agent system testing examines systems in which several AI agents act on shared tasks or resources, to find failures that no single agent shows on its own. Testers run the agents together in simulated or scripted scenarios, often with injected faults such as failed sensors, delayed messages or conflicting goals, and record the failures that appear. Checks cover whether the task is completed, whether coordination breaks down (for example through deadlock, collisions or one agent's error spreading to others), and whether stated safety rules are ever broken. For language-model agents, benchmarks such as MultiAgentBench score task completion and the quality of collaboration or competition. For small or abstract models, a model checker such as MCMAS can search every reachable state for a violation of a rule written in formal logic and, for many kinds of rule, return an example run that breaks it.

example_use_cases.description: A logistics firm models its warehouse robots' movement rules in a model checker and asks whether two robots can ever occupy the same aisle cell or wait on each other forever. Any counterexample the checker returns is a concrete sequence of events that engineers replay in simulation before the control software goes live.

A city traffic authority testing coordinated intersection controllers injects sensor failures and conflicting local objectives in a simulator. It checks whether emergency vehicles still get priority and traffic flow stays within agreed limits, and decides from the results whether the system can go to a pilot corridor.

A trading firm's risk team runs all of its cooperating trading agents together in a market simulator replaying a high-volatility day. It checks whether their combined orders breach position limits or form patterns that compliance would treat as manipulation, and whether one agent's failure spreads to the others.

A software company building a team of language-model agents to fix bugs (a planner, a coder and a reviewer) runs the team on a benchmark of shared coding tasks under different coordination layouts, such as a chain or a star. It compares task completion and coordination scores before choosing a layout for production.

limitations.description: The number of possible interactions grows explosively with the number of agents, so tests sample a tiny part of the space. A clean run shows that the scenarios tried did not fail, not that none will, and the gap widens as agents are added.

Model checking needs a formal model of each agent and its environment, and the answer is only as good as that model. Large state spaces limit how many agents it can handle, and agents that learn and change behaviour are hard to capture, so it is usually combined with simulation testing.

Benchmark scores for communication and planning come from a language model acting as judge on a coarse five-point scale, so they inherit its biases. A high coordination score does not show that a safety property holds.

Simulators simplify real conditions such as communication delays, sensor noise and physical or social dynamics, and realistic simulation is costly to build and needs domain modelling expertise. Failures that occur only in the real environment will not appear.

Tests and model checks find only the failures the testers specify. A hazard that no one wrote a safety rule or scenario for is not tested, and rules written in temporal logic need specialist skill to state correctly.

resources.title: MCMAS: an open-source model checker for the verification of multi-agent systems
resources.abstract: We present MCMAS, a model checker for the verification of multi-agent systems. MCMAS supports efficient symbolic techniques for the verification of multi-agent systems against specifications representing temporal, epistemic and strategic properties. We present the underlying semantics of the specification language supported and the algorithms implemented in MCMAS, including its fairness and counterexample generation features. We provide a detailed description of the implementation. We illustrate its use by discussing a number of examples and evaluate its performance by comparing it against other model checkers for multi-agent systems on a common case study.

resources.title: MultiAgentBench : Evaluating the Collaboration and Competition of LLM agents
resources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities as autonomous agents, yet existing benchmarks either focus on single-agent tasks or are confined to narrow domains, failing to capture the dynamics of multi-agent coordination and competition. In this paper, we introduce MultiAgentBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate LLM-based multi-agent systems across diverse, interactive scenarios. Our framework measures not only task completion but also the quality of collaboration and competition using novel, milestone-based key performance indicators. Moreover, we evaluate various coordination protocols (including star, chain, tree, and graph topologies) and innovative strategies such as group discussion and cognitive planning. Notably, gpt-4o-mini reaches the average highest task score, graph structure performs the best among coordination protocols in the research scenario, and cognitive planning improves milestone achievement rates by 3%. Code and datasets are public available at https://github.com/MultiagentBench/MARBLE.

resources.title: RV4JaCa - Towards Runtime Verification of Multi-Agent Systems and Robotic Applications
resources.abstract: This paper presents a Runtime Verification (RV) approach for Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) using the JaCaMo framework. Our objective is to bring a layer of security to the MAS. This is achieved keeping in mind possible safety-critical uses of the MAS, such as robotic applications. This layer is capable of controlling events during the execution of the system without needing a specific implementation in the behaviour of each agent to recognise the events. In this paper, we mainly focus on MAS when used in the context of hybrid intelligence. This use requires communication between software agents and human beings. In some cases, communication takes place via natural language dialogues. However, this kind of communication brings us to a concern related to controlling the flow of dialogue so that agents can prevent any change in the topic of discussion that could impair their reasoning. The latter may be a problem and undermine the development of the software agents. In this paper, we tackle this problem by proposing and demonstrating the implementation of a framework that aims to control the dialogue flow in a MAS; especially when the MAS communicates with the user through natural language to aid decision-making in a hospital bed allocation scenario.

techniques.name: Model Signing
techniques.description: Model signing lets the publisher of a machine-learning model attach a cryptographic signature to the model's files, so that anyone who later loads them can check who released them and that no file has changed since. Under the Open Source Security Foundation's Model Signing (OMS) specification and its reference tool, model-signing, the publisher computes a hash (a short fingerprint that changes if a single byte of the file changes) of every file in the model directory, such as weights, configuration, tokeniser and any dataset files kept with them, lists the hashes in a sorted manifest and signs the manifest, producing a detached signature file kept beside the model. The signature can be made with the publisher's own key, with a certificate from an organisation's certificate authority, or through Sigstore, which issues a short-lived certificate tied to a verified online identity, such as a person's account or a build pipeline's, and records each signing event in a transparency log, an append-only record that can be inspected afterwards. Before loading, the consumer verifies the signature against the signer it expects, recomputes every hash and rejects the model if any listed file differs or is missing or, unless that check is switched off, an unlisted file has appeared, so the evidence is a pass or fail tied to a named signer and an exact set of files. Unlike the unsigned file hashes kept by data-versioning tools, it shows who stands behind the files, and unlike a watermark, which is trained into the weights so that it survives in an altered copy, it is broken by any change; it says nothing about how the model behaves or what it was trained on.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's machine-learning platform team signs each model at the end of its training pipeline, using the pipeline's own workload identity through Sigstore, and configures its model-serving cluster to load only models whose signature verifies against that identity. Its security team watches the transparency log for signing events under that identity that match no approved release, to decide whether a model reached production outside the release process.

A vehicle maker's perception team downloads a pretrained object detector from a supplier catalogue that signs every model it publishes. Before fine-tuning, it verifies the download against the supplier's published certificate and files the verification output in its supplier-acceptance record, so later reviews can show exactly which files the work started from.

A hospital's imaging department receives quarterly updates to a vendor's chest X-ray triage model. Its clinical engineering team verifies each update against the vendor's certificate and rejects any update whose signature fails, or that contains a file the signature does not cover, before it enters the clinical validation environment.

A public research institute releases an open model together with the test set behind its published benchmark, signing both in one bundle, so that a laboratory re-running the benchmark can confirm that the weights and the test data are byte for byte the ones the institute released before comparing its results with the published ones.

limitations.description: It shows who released the files and that they have not changed, nothing more. A model carrying a malicious pickle payload, a backdoor or the effects of poisoned training data verifies perfectly if its publisher signed it, whether through carelessness or because the publisher's own pipeline was compromised before signing. The originating paper states that signing tells the user nothing about what a model does or how it was produced, so content checks are still needed.

A valid signature is only as good as the consumer's check of who made it. A model signed with an attacker's own identity, or by an account named to look like a well-known organisation (a documented attack on model hubs), verifies cleanly unless the verifier insists on the specific identity, certificate or public key it expects. Consumers need a maintained list of trusted signers for each model source.

A stolen signing key, or a compromised account at the identity provider used for Sigstore signing, produces valid signatures. With Sigstore every signature is recorded in a transparency log, so a publisher that monitors the log for its own identity can spot signatures it did not make; with the key and certificate methods the specification does not require a log entry, so misuse of a key may go unnoticed.

Any change to the files breaks verification, including legitimate ones such as quantisation, conversion to another file format or adding a file. Each derived model needs a new signature from whoever produced it, and that signature says nothing about how the derivative relates to the signed original; recording that relationship needs a separate provenance record, such as the pedigree section of an ML-BOM.

It protects only where verification is enforced. Most models on public hubs are unsigned (fewer than 2% of Hugging Face models used the hub's GPG commit-signing option, per studies the originating paper cites), and an unchecked signature protects nobody. Verification re-hashes every file, and hashing dominates the cost: a 1 TB file took about 13 minutes on a 128-vCPU server in the originating paper's benchmark, which matters if very large models are verified at every load.

resources.title: Position: Machine Learning Models Have a Supply Chain Problem
resources.abstract: Powerful machine learning (ML) models are now readily available online, which creates exciting possibilities for users who lack the deep technical expertise or substantial computing resources needed to develop them. On the other hand, this type of open ecosystem comes with many risks. In this paper, we argue that the current ecosystem for open ML models contains significant supply-chain risks, some of which have been exploited already in real attacks. These include an attacker replacing a model with something malicious (e.g., malware), or a model being trained using a vulnerable version of a framework or on restricted or poisoned data. We then explore how Sigstore, a solution designed to bring transparency to open-source software supply chains, can be used to bring transparency to open ML models, in terms of enabling model publishers to sign their models and prove properties about the datasets they use.

techniques.name: Signal Temporal Logic Monitoring
techniques.description: Signal temporal logic (STL) monitoring checks the signals a system produces over time, such as speeds, distances, positions or a model's outputs, against safety requirements written in signal temporal logic, a formal language for stating how real-valued signals must behave over time intervals (for example, 'whenever the gap to the vehicle ahead falls below 10 m, speed drops below 5 m/s within 2 s'). Each requirement is built from comparisons of signals with thresholds, joined by logical operators and by timed operators such as 'always within [a, b]', 'eventually within [a, b]' and 'until'. For each trace the monitor computes a robustness value, a margin to the requirement rather than robustness to adversarial inputs: its sign says whether the requirement is met (positive) or violated (negative), and its size is a tolerance: any signal whose values stay closer than that to the observed ones at every instant gets the same verdict. Monitors run offline on logged or simulated traces, or online on live signals, where a requirement that looks ahead in time can be decided only once enough of the signal has arrived. RTAMT, the named tool, is an open-source Python library with an optional C++ back-end that builds such monitors from a written specification and connects to ROS and MATLAB/Simulink; its online monitors accept only requirements whose future time windows are bounded and give each verdict after a delay equal to the requirement's time horizon, and it reports the robustness value but does not act on it, so stopping or correcting the system is left to a separate safeguard.

example_use_cases.description: A team developing an adaptive cruise controller with a learned speed policy writes its requirements in STL, for example that the time gap to the vehicle ahead never stays below one second for longer than two seconds, and attaches an RTAMT monitor to every drive in an urban driving simulator. The robustness values show which controller settings meet each requirement and by what margin, and drives with negative values become regression scenarios.

A hospital's service robot, which uses learned perception to find people, fetches supplies along corridors. The integrator monitors live ROS topics against a system requirement (always at least 0.5 m from any detected person) and against one requirement per subsystem, such as the planner reaching its next waypoint in time. When a subsystem requirement fails shortly before the system one, the logged verdicts show where the fault began.

A drone-delivery operator checks each day's flight logs from its learned landing controller against a requirement that, in the last ten seconds before touchdown, descent rate stays below 1 m/s and the drone stays within 0.5 m of the pad centre. It reports the smallest robustness value across all landings to its safety manager and investigates any landing whose value is negative.

limitations.description: The monitor checks the requirement as written, not as intended. Writing correct STL needs fluency in the logic and in the system: a wrong threshold, a time window that is too short or a misplaced operator yields confident positive margins for behaviour the engineers would call unsafe, and nothing in the monitor reveals the mistake. Specifications need the same review as the requirements they encode.

Online monitoring judges a requirement from a partial trace. RTAMT's online monitors take only requirements whose future time windows are bounded, and give each verdict after a delay equal to the requirement's horizon: a check that something happens within five seconds is decided five seconds later, which may be too late to act on in a fast system. Monitors that track a narrowing range of possible robustness values can flag some violations sooner, but stay undecided until the data settles it.

A robustness value is measured in the units of the signals in the requirement, so a margin of 0.4 means 0.4 metres in one requirement and 0.4 degrees in another. Values cannot be compared across requirements, and when one requirement combines signals of different scales its value is set by whichever margin is numerically smallest, which depends on the units chosen unless the signals are normalised first.

Monitoring reports on the traces it sees. A clean record over many hours shows that those runs met the requirement, not that every possible run will, and a violation is reported when it happens, not before, unless a separate predictor of future signals is added. To protect the system, the verdict has to drive a safeguard such as a fallback controller, which the monitor does not provide.

The verdict is only as good as the signals. If a learned perception component misjudges the distance to a person, the monitor computes a confident margin from the wrong distance; independent sensors or ground truth are needed to check the perception itself. Discrete-time monitors see only the samples taken, so a brief violation between samples can go unseen, and the ROS integration assumes messages arrive at a known, regular rate.

techniques.name: Metamorphic Testing
techniques.description: Metamorphic testing checks a model or AI system without needing the correct output for each test input, by checking that the outputs for related inputs stand in a relation that must hold if the system works as intended. The tester first writes metamorphic relations from knowledge of the task, each pairing a change to the input with the change it should cause in the output, or with no change: adding fog to a road image should leave a steering prediction within a set tolerance, adding a few stray sensor points outside the road area should not remove any detected obstacle, and rotating a whole flight scenario should leave its outcome unchanged. Existing test inputs (source cases) are transformed into follow-up inputs according to each relation, the system is run on both, and each pair is checked, with numeric outputs often allowed a tolerance. A violation points to a fault or unwanted behaviour without any labelled answer, unless the relation itself is wrong; the output is the violation rate for each relation with the failing pairs, and a relation that holds on every pair shows only that the outputs agree with each other, not that they are right. Prompt robustness testing and causal discrimination testing in this catalogue each apply one family of invariance relations (meaning-preserving changes to a prompt, and a change of protected attribute), and prompt robustness testing also scores the answers against known ones; metamorphic testing is the general procedure for writing and checking any such relation, including relations that say how the output should change, and needs no known answers.

example_use_cases.description: An air navigation service provider evaluating a machine-learning conflict-detection aid for en-route controllers has no ground truth for most replayed traffic samples. Its test team writes three relations: swapping two aircraft's call signs, shifting every timestamp by the same amount, and rotating the whole sample together with its wind field must not change which aircraft pairs are flagged. It runs them on a year of recorded traffic and holds the release until every violation is explained.

A supplier of lidar obstacle perception for driverless shuttles cannot label every frame it records. Following a relation implied by the perception specification, its test team adds a few hundred random points outside the mapped road area to recorded frames and checks that no obstacle detected in the original frame disappears, reporting the share of frames where one does, by number of points added, as a release criterion for each software build.

A weather service testing a neural network that nowcasts rainfall from radar images checks a relation expected from the way rain moves with the wind: away from the domain's edges, shifting the input radar sequence a few grid cells east should shift the forecast rain field by the same amount, within a tolerance set from the model's day-to-day error. Forecasters review the breaking cases to judge whether the model has learnt a dependence on location, such as on terrain, that it should keep.

A bank moving its credit-scoring models to a new library cannot treat every difference from the old library's outputs as a fault, since the solvers differ. Its validation team writes relations the mathematics guarantees: reordering the input columns, or adding a constant to a numeric input in training and scoring data of a logistic regression with an unpenalised intercept, must leave every predicted probability unchanged within solver tolerance. Each violation is investigated as a fault.

limitations.description: Passing shows that outputs are consistent, not that they are correct. A model that gives the same wrong answer for a source case and its follow-up satisfies the relation, and one that is wrong in the same way everywhere can pass every invariance relation. On its own the technique therefore does not suit systems where each output must be shown to be right, and it complements rather than replaces testing against known answers where those exist.

The evidence is only as good as the relations, which are written by hand from domain knowledge, with no systematic way to choose among the many possible ones. A relation the system is not bound to obey produces false alarms: in a study of the Weka library, violations by its nearest-neighbour classifier came from legitimate tie-breaking between equally likely labels, not from faults. An incomplete set of relations gives false confidence.

Most model outputs need a tolerance, and the result depends heavily on it. In the DeepTest study of three driving models, violations under simple image transformations fell from 23,391 when a transformed frame's squared error against the human steering label could be at most the original mean squared error to 330 when it could be five times that, and manual review still found false positives. Counts compare only between runs with the same tolerance, set from what the application can accept.

Follow-up inputs are synthetic and may not occur in practice: rain or fog added to an image, or points scattered into a lidar frame, approximate real conditions without reproducing them. A violation on an unrealistic input may not matter in operation, and a pass covers only the transformations tried, so the evidence is about the tested relations and transformations, not the operating conditions as a whole.

A model whose outputs vary between runs on the same input, through sampling, seeds or GPU arithmetic, breaks relations by chance, so runs must be made repeatable or each case repeated and judged statistically. This bites hardest for relations over the training data, such as Xie et al.'s for classifiers, which need the model retrained for every follow-up case; for models that are costly to train only prediction-time relations are practical, and they test the trained model, not its training.

resources.title: Metamorphic Testing: A New Approach for Generating Next Test Cases
resources.abstract: In software testing, a set of test cases is constructed according to some predefined selection criteria. The software is then examined against these test cases. Three interesting observations have been made on the current artifacts of software testing. Firstly, an error-revealing test case is considered useful while a successful test case which does not reveal software errors is usually not further investigated. Whether these successful test cases still contain useful information for revealing software errors has not been properly studied. Secondly, no matter how extensive the testing has been conducted in the development phase, errors may still exist in the software [5]. These errors, if left undetected, may eventually cause damage to the production system. The study of techniques for uncovering software errors in the production phase is seldom addressed in the literature. Thirdly, as indicated by Weyuker in [6], the availability of test oracles is pragmatically unattainable in most situations. However, the availability of test oracles is generally assumed in conventional software testing techniques. In this paper, we propose a novel test case selection technique that derives new test cases from the successful ones. The selection aims at revealing software errors that are possibly left undetected in successful test cases which may be generated using some existing strategies. As such, the proposed technique augments the effectiveness of existing test selection strategies. The technique also helps uncover software errors in the production phase and can be used in the absence of test oracles.

techniques.name: Explainer Latency Benchmarking
techniques.description: Explainer latency benchmarking measures how long an explanation method takes to produce an explanation for a single prediction, on the hardware, software and settings it will run with, and compares the result with the time that the decision it supports allows. The evaluator first sets the time budget, the share of the time the decision allows that is left for the explanation once the prediction is ready, then runs the explainer exactly as it will be deployed (the same model, background data, number of samples and batch size) on a representative set of real inputs, timing each explanation from request to a result ready to display, after warm-up runs and with one-off set-up costs, such as building the explainer, recorded separately. Because the time varies with the model, the data, the hardware and the load on the system, each configuration is timed many times, as machine-learning inference benchmarks such as MLPerf Inference time a model, under realistic concurrent demand where the explainer runs as a shared service, and the result is reported as a distribution: the median, high percentiles such as the 95th or 99th, the slowest case and the share of explanations over budget. Canha et al.'s benchmark framework for explanation methods, which scores methods on properties measurable without human participants, includes this property under the name speed and rates it on a five-level scale with cut-offs at 0.1, 1, 5 and 10 seconds aligned with human response-time limits; the scale suits comparisons between methods, while a claim about a deployment needs the measured percentiles set against that deployment's own budget. The output is a latency profile for each explainer configuration, recorded with its hardware, software versions and load, which shows whether explanations will arrive in time and lets a team choose between explainers and settings on speed alongside the explanation quality measured by other tests.

example_use_cases.description: A card issuer shows its fraud analysts a feature attribution beside each held transaction and needs it within the two seconds before the review queue refreshes. Benchmarking on the production server at peak queue load, it finds that a sampling-based explainer misses the budget for about one explanation in twenty while an explainer specific to its tree ensemble stays well inside it, and adopts the second once its attributions pass the same faithfulness tests.

A hospital adding an explanation panel to a sepsis-risk alert in its electronic health record agrees with clinicians that the panel must load within one second of a nurse opening the alert. The informatics team times explanations on the hospital's own servers with a week of real alerts at typical volume, reports the 95th percentile and the slowest case against that limit, and repeats the measurement after each model or software update.

An online marketplace shows each seller the main reasons its moderation model held a new listing for review, and the page must update within three seconds. Before launch, the team times the service on its production servers with a week of recorded traffic replayed at its real pace; the first request after each quiet period is far slower because the explainer and its background data load on demand. It keeps a loaded explainer running, re-measures, and reports the slowest case.

limitations.description: Speed and explanation quality trade off through the explainer's settings. Sampling-based explainers run faster with fewer samples or a smaller background dataset, but SHAP's documentation notes that more samples give lower-variance estimates, so a faster setting gives noisier explanations. A latency result holds only for the settings tested, and must be measured at the settings whose faithfulness and stability were checked, or a configuration may meet the budget with untested explanations.

Times depend on the hardware, the implementation and the load at the moment of measurement, which Canha et al. single out as the main caveat on their speed metric, so a figure from a developer's workstation does not carry over to a shared production server or an edge device. Any change to the model, the explainer version, the hardware or the traffic pattern calls for re-measurement, and the configuration must be recorded with the result for it to be checked or repeated.

Claims about the slowest cases need many timed explanations. MLPerf Inference, which sets tail-latency bounds for model inference in the same way, sizes its runs so that a 99th-percentile bound holds with 99 per cent confidence, which at its chosen margin takes about 263,000 queries. A few hundred timings can support a claim about the median but not about the 99th percentile, and a single timed run supports neither.

A fast explanation is not necessarily a good one. Latency says nothing about whether an explanation reflects what the model did or whether people can use it, and it leaves out the time a person needs to read it. It supports a claim about explanations only alongside tests of faithfulness and stability and, where people act on the explanations, a study of whether they can use them within the time available.

The budget has to come from the decision, not from a generic scale. Canha et al.'s cut-offs reflect general limits on human response time, which may be looser or tighter than a particular workflow allows, and a budget that leaves out the time to run the model, move the data and display the result will be met in the benchmark and missed in use; MLPerf likewise derives its server-scenario latency bounds from the user's overall time target.

techniques.name: C2PA Content Credentials
techniques.description: C2PA Content Credentials attach a signed provenance record, called a manifest, to a media file, so that whoever receives the file can see who signed it and what the signer declares (which tool produced it, whether a generative AI model created or altered it and what edits followed), and can check that the record, and the parts of the file its hash covers, have not changed since signing. Under the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) technical specification, the tool that creates or edits the file writes statements called assertions, such as a 'created' action whose source type is trainedAlgorithmicMedia (the code for AI-generated content) and links to the earlier files it was made from, adds a cryptographic hash of the file's content, and signs the bundle with an X.509 certificate, the kind of credential used to secure websites. The manifest is usually embedded in the file, and each later edit in a supporting tool adds a new manifest that refers to the previous one, so the history travels with the file. A validator recomputes the hash and checks the signature, then reports the manifest as well-formed, valid or, if the signing certificate chains to a trust list such as the C2PA Trust List, trusted, and reports a failure when the file no longer matches its hash. If the manifest is removed, nothing in the file leads back to it unless a watermark or fingerprint (a 'soft binding') was also registered so that the manifest can be looked up in a repository, and a file without credentials says nothing about its origin; unlike trigger-set model watermarking or model signing, which mark or sign a model, it records the history of an individual output.

example_use_cases.description: An image-generation service offered in the EU attaches a signed manifest to every image it returns, declaring an AI 'created' action with the service as signer, as its means of meeting the AI Act's Article 50(2) duty to mark synthetic output in a machine-readable format. Its compliance team validates a weekly sample of outputs to decide whether marking is working, and registers a watermark soft binding so that a stripped image can be matched back to its record.

A news agency's verification desk runs every image sent in by the public through a C2PA validator before publication. A trusted manifest recording capture on a named camera, with no AI-generated ingredients, lets editors publish it with a provenance label. A manifest naming a generative tool, or a hash that no longer matches, sends it to forensic review, and an image with no credentials is treated as of unknown origin, not as authentic.

An insurer's claims app lets assessors apply an AI tool that enhances and annotates photographs of vehicle damage, and records each AI edit as an action in the photograph's manifest. When a claim is disputed, a reviewing assessor or the claimant's representative can see which changes the AI tool made and check them against the retained original, which the edited photograph's manifest cites as an ingredient.

A social-media platform reads Content Credentials on upload, labels images whose trusted manifest declares a generative AI source, and shows users who signed the record. Its trust-and-safety team tracks what share of uploads carry trusted, untrusted or no credentials, to decide how far its synthetic-media policy can rely on the labels and where it still needs other detection methods.

limitations.description: The record is easy to lose. Anyone can remove the manifest, an attack the C2PA's own threat model expects, and the file is then an ordinary file with no link to its history unless a watermark or fingerprint soft binding was registered with a manifest repository. Because credentials are optional and removable, a file without them says nothing about its origin: the absence of a manifest cannot show that content is human-made or unaltered.

A valid manifest shows who signed the record and that what its hash covers is unchanged, not that its statements are true. A signer can omit an AI step, a stolen key yields manifests that validate, and a camera photographing a screen signs a genuine capture of a staged scene. Validators need not check revocation, metadata such as location may sit outside the hash, and a 2026 preprint found validators disagreeing on the same file, so a result depends on the signer, validator and trust list.

The history is complete only while every tool in the workflow supports C2PA. An edit made in an unsupported tool is not recorded, and if the file later passes through a supporting tool, the new signer implicitly vouches for that unrecorded change, so the chain can show fewer steps than took place. The C2PA itself says the approach depends on widespread adoption by tools and platforms.

Manifests can disclose more than the creator intends, such as capture time and place, device details, the edit history and, through the separate Creator Assertions Working Group identity extension, who made the content. The C2PA's threat model lists identifying creators and tracking viewers as risks. Assertions can be redacted when a file is reused as an ingredient, but people working in risky settings, such as human-rights documentation, must decide what to include before signing.

Support for AI-generated text is immature. Embedding a manifest in plain text, as invisible Unicode characters, entered the specification in version 2.3 and is still marked as under review; the reference SDK supports it only behind an unstable option, and any edit to the text breaks the hash. For language-model output the method is much less dependable than for images, video and audio, where embedding is established.

sample_claims.text: Every image in each weekly validation sample of the generation service's output carried a C2PA manifest, signed with a certificate that chains to the C2PA Trust List, that declares the image AI-generated.
In the provider's stripping and re-encoding tests, generated images whose embedded manifest had been removed were matched to their original manifest through the registered watermark soft binding.
Every reader-submitted image published with a provenance label had a trusted manifest whose hash matched the published file.
Each AI edit applied to a claims photograph is recorded as an action in the photograph's signed manifest, naming the tool that made it.
